title: Opinion Verbs: Saying You Do Not Think So

sections.title: Where the "no" goes
sections.content: You know *creo que* + indicative and *no creo que* + subjunctive from B1 Unit 7, and *dudo que* from B1 Unit 13. The rule is simple: an opinion you hold is stated as a fact, so it takes the indicative; an opinion you reject is not stated as a fact, so it takes the subjunctive. At B2 you apply this to the whole family of opinion verbs (*pensar*, *opinar*, *considerar*, *parecer*), and you learn that the mood depends on where the *no* stands.

sections.title: Opinion verbs and mood
rows: Pienso que tiene razón. / Me parece que tiene razón.
No pienso que tenga razón. / No me parece que tenga razón.
The no belongs to the second verb, so the opinion verb is affirmative: indicative.
In the past, the subjunctive moves back too: imperfect subjunctive.

sections.title: Two ways to say almost the same thing
sections.content: English 'I don't think he is coming' can be *Creo que no viene* or *No creo que venga*. Both are correct, but they are built differently: in the first one the opinion verb is affirmative, so the verb after it is in the indicative; in the second one the opinion verb is negated, so the verb after it is in the subjunctive. Choose the mood by looking at where the *no* is.

items.spanish: Pienso que la idea es buena.
items.english: I think the idea is good.

items.spanish: No pienso que la idea sea buena.
items.english: I don't think the idea is good.

items.spanish: Creo que no es una buena idea.
items.english: I think it is not a good idea.

items.spanish: No me parece que tenga razón.
items.english: It doesn't seem to me that he is right.
I didn't think it was true.

sections.content: Only the opinion verb decides the mood. Once a *no* stands in front of it (*no creo*, *no pienso*, *no me parece*), the subjunctive follows. Verbs of doubt work the other way round, as you will see in the next lesson.
